[MUJAHID:v2p497#4/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says the abode of the Hereafter is a life in which there is no death.
[MUQATIL:29:64-68/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Worldly life is only falsehood, pastime, and play.
[MUQATIL:29:64-68/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The hereafter is Paradise, the home of real life where there is no death.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p640/r5] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The worldly people meant here are the polytheists, who want nothing beyond this life and deny the afterlife.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p640/r6] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | The hereafter meant here is Paradise.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p640/r7] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · ابن مجاهد | reports | Ibn Mujahid, from his father, says the afterlife is life without death: its inhabitants remain and never die.
[YAHYA-SALLAM:v2p640/r8] YAHYA-SALLAM, d. 200 · author | holds | If the polytheists knew the truth, they would know that the afterlife is better than this world.

[TAB-FULL:v18p440/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The afterlife contains enduring life without disappearance, interruption, or death.

[IBNABIHATIM:v9p3080#3/r8] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas says the Hereafter is enduring.
[IBNABIHATIM:v9p3080#3/r9] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · مجاهد | reports | Mujahid says there is no death in the Hereafter.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The poem's zafiyān witnesses an adjectival pattern like ṣamiyān, supporting the adjective analysis.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r11] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | As a verbal noun, the phrase means the Hereafter's life is true life, without the deficiency and ending that mar worldly life.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r12] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Alternatively, the Hereafter is called living because it neither vanishes nor perishes; the description refers to its inhabitants.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | The Hereafter is the abode of life in which its inhabitants do not die.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · قتادة والسدي | reports | Qatāda and al-Suddī gloss al-ḥayawān as life.

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba say al-ḥayawān means life; exegetes and semantic scholars agree on that sense here.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | reports | Reporting Abū ʿUbayda, Abū ʿAlī says al-ḥayāt, al-ḥayawān, and al-ḥayy are verbal nouns.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd says ḥayawān can mean any animate thing, the opposite of lifeless matter; it may be an adjective rather than a verbal noun.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p555#3/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Al-ḥayawān may be a verbal noun per Abū ʿUbayda or an adjective per Abū Zayd, comparable to ṣamiyān and zafiyān.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p558/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The phrase can mean the Hereafter is the abode possessing life, as if worldly life did not count as life.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p558/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الخليل وسيبويه وأصحابهما | reports | Al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, and their colleagues derive the wāw by changing the second of two root yāʾs, since this pattern does not allow assimilation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p558/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو عثمان | reports | Abū ʿUthmān says the wāw is original and al-ḥayawān is a verbal noun without a corresponding verb, like fawẓ.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p558/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | rejects | Abū ʿAlī rejects Abū ʿUthmān's analogy: words with medial wāw and a sound final exist, but the proposed yāʾ-medial, wāw-final pattern does not.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p558/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو علي | holds | The name Ḥaywa, as in Rajāʾ b. Ḥaywa, originally had a final yāʾ changed to wāw to avoid doubling; proper names permit such extensions.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v17p560/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | If they understood, they would choose what lasts over what passes away; they do not understand.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:29:63-67/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | This worldly life is diversion and play because it soon passes away, while the hereafter is lasting life; they fail to know that permanence.
[JISHUMI:v8p5590/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda says al-hayawān and al-ḥayāh both mean life and are verbal nouns of ḥayya.
[JISHUMI:v8p5590/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Life is an accident that unifies the parts of a thing so it can be knowing and powerful; its defining property is perception.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p255/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Leisure is enjoyment of worldly pleasures and play is frivolity; the world is called these because it is transient.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p255/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Al-hayawan means life: the afterlife contains enduring, permanent life.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v6p255/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | If they knew, they would recognize that this world perishes and the afterlife remains.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p325/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Worldly pursuits beyond what sustains life and strength for obedience are diversion and play; what is done for God belongs to the afterlife.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p325/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Rich and poor share the same necessities: breathing, relieving hunger, covering nakedness, and protection from heat and cold.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p325/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh treat ḥayawān as a verbal noun synonymous with ḥayāh, like hayamān.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v4p325/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · مجاهد | prefers | Mujāhid explains the afterlife as a life with no death; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this good.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p283#2/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Worldly life is a deception that passes away shortly.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p283#2/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The Hereafter means Paradise, the abode of life without death or the defects that accompany worldly life.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p283#2/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda regards the lām in lahiya as an extra particle of emphasis.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v6p283#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abū ʿUbayda says ḥayawān and ḥayāh both mean life.

[RAZI-FULL:v25p80#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, the afterlife earns this name because it contains increase and growth and is where full, true perception occurs. | mentions 10:26, 86:9
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Because people acknowledge God as creator and provider yet leave worship for worldly adornment, al-Razi says God shows that what attracts them is nothing.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | One distinction is that play means turning toward falsehood for fleeting pleasure, while lahw means turning away from truth; worldly life involves both.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Alternatively, play is putting one activity first and intending to do the other later, while lahw is becoming absorbed in one and turning wholly from the other.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Chess and pigeon keeping are not conventionally called instruments of lahw, but stringed instruments are because their immediate pleasure distracts a person from everything else.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | For some people worldly life is play: they engage in it expecting to turn to worship and the afterlife later; for others it is lahw, and they forget the afterlife entirely.
[RAZI-FULL:v25p80/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The demonstrative “this” fits the present context because it has just mentioned worldly life through the earth revived by rain; in the cited regret passage, the preceding scene is the afterlife, so it says simply “worldly life.” | mentions 2:164, 6:31, 3:185
[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r10] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · أبو عبيدة | reports | Abu Ubayda equates al-ḥayawān with life and the word ḥayy with a kasra; an anonymous poetic line illustrates the usage of ḥayāt.
[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r11] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · غيره | reports | Others explain ḥayy as a plural on the pattern fuʿūl, like ʿuṣiyy.

[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r15] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The closing clause means that they would know the afterlife is truly the enduring life if they understood.

[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r7] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | This criticism concerns worldly wealth, status, and clothing beyond basic needs and the means needed to sustain life and obey God.
[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r8] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | What is done for God belongs to the afterlife and endures, meaning what is sought for His reward and pleasure. | mentions 55:27
[QURTUBI-FULL:29:63-64/r9] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | The afterlife is the lasting abode of life: it does not pass away and contains no death.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Calling this life insignificant expresses contempt; with God it weighs less than a mosquito's wing.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Worldly life resembles children's play: they gather and enjoy it briefly, then part exhausted.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | reports | The afterlife is true life because death cannot reach it, or it is life itself by an intensive expression.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ḥayawān is a verbal noun of ḥayya used for a living being; originally ḥayayan, its second yāʾ changed to wāw.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r5] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Ḥayawān is more emphatic than ḥayāh because faʿalān suggests life's movement and agitation.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:29:64-65/r6] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | If they knew, they would not prefer worldly life, whose life is incidental, brief, and rooted in nonlife.

[NASAFI-FULL:v3p265/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Lahw is a pleasure that distracts someone briefly and then ends.
[NASAFI-FULL:v3p265/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The world is so slight that, with God, it does not weigh a mosquito's wing.

[NASAFI-FULL:v3p265/r8] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | If they knew the nature of both abodes, they would not prefer fleeting amusement to lasting life.

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p366/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الخليل وسيبويه | reports | Al-Khalīl and Sībawayh take الحيوان as the verbal noun of حيِيَ; here it means the enduring abode of life. Mujāhid says there is no death there; another explanation calls the living person by the verbal noun.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v8p366/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The afterlife is called حیّاً hyperbolically for its life; فعلان marks movement and agitation, and the لو clause leaves its answer implicit: people would not choose the perishable if they knew.

[SAMIN-DURR:29:64/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · سيبويه وأتباعه | reports | Sibawayh and followers derive واو in الحيوان from ياء by anomalous replacement, as also in proper name حيوة.

[SAMIN-DURR:29:64/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | Others take the form at face value, with واو as root-final; حيي does not disprove Sibawayh because واو becomes ياء after kasra.
[SAMIN-DURR:29:64/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | If they knew the afterlife is the true life, they would not prefer this world over it.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p294#3/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | The worldly life is trivial, passing, and short-lived; the Hereafter is the real, enduring life that never ends.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v6p294#3/r2] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | If people understood, they would choose what remains over what perishes.

[BURHAN:v1p120/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In al-Aʿraf, amusement comes first because the passage concerns the Day of Judgment and orders the two states by what has just ended.

[BURHAN:v1p407#2/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The incompleteness of worldly existence compared with the afterlife is illustrated by calling the latter the true life. | mentions 29:64
